AT0064.title: Infostealers
AT0064.description: Infostealers are a class of malware specifically designed to steal sensitive information from victim devices, primarily targeting browser-saved passwords, cookies, autofill data, and cryptocurrency wallet keys. Representative families include RedLine, Raccoon, Vidar, LummaC2 (Lumma), StealC, and Meta. In 2025-2026, infostealers have become the top threat for global data breaches, with single incidents leading to billions of credentials being leaked. Main functions include: (1) Browser data theft: extracting saved login credentials, cookies, credit card information, and autofill data from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and other browsers. (2) Cryptocurrency wallet theft: searching for and stealing key files and mnemonic phrases from MetaMask, Exodus, and other wallets. (3) Session token theft: stealing session tokens from Discord, Telegram, Steam, and other applications for password-free login. (4) Screenshots and keylogging: periodically capturing screen content and recording keyboard input to harvest unsaved credentials. (5) System information collection: gathering OS version, hardware information, and installed software lists. (6) Data exfiltration: sending stolen data through encrypted channels to attacker-controlled servers or Telegram bots. Infostealers typically spread through phishing emails, fake software downloads, cracked software, and fake VPN applications, with stolen data sold in bulk on dark web markets as 'logs'.

AT0064-001.title: Keyloggers
AT0064-001.description:
A keylogger records keyboard input to steal passwords, payment data, chat content, and other sensitive information. Major software implementations include API hooks such as SetWindowsHookEx, kernel drivers that capture input below user space, form grabbing before browser submission, and screen-recording assistance for virtual keyboards, verification codes, or input positions. Modern software keyloggers commonly operate as modules in infostealers or are embedded in legitimate applications as spyware, and can exfiltrate results through email, FTP, HTTP, or messaging bots.

Hardware keyloggers can sit between a USB keyboard and a computer or be embedded inside a keyboard enclosure or USB hub, parsing HID data outside the target operating system. Some open-source devices provide circular flash storage, Wi-Fi management, AES-encrypted logs, scheduled remote delivery, and automatic attempts to use open wireless networks. Because they do not need to create a process, driver, or file on the target host, antivirus and EDR products may not directly observe the recording activity. Peripheral inventory, USB-port seals, cable and keyboard inspection, rogue-hotspot scanning, anomalous network connections, and physical office inspections can still reveal an implant.
